s.line: All this time Dorothy and her companions had been walking through the thick woods.
s.note: סָבוּךְ (thick, tangled) is a pa'ul participle: "entangled". From the same root: מְסֻבָּךְ = complicated, an everyday word (זֶה מְסֻבָּךְ = it's complicated). וַחֲבֵרֶיהָ: before a letter with חֲ the "and" prefix takes the same vowel, וַ.

w: בְּמִדָּה רַבָּה|to a great extent|~lit. in a large measure
s.line: The road was still paved with yellow brick, but these were much covered by dried branches and dead leaves from the trees,
s.note: Two pu'al participles: מְרֻצֶּפֶת (paved; רִצְפָּה = floor) and מְכֻסּוֹת (covered; pi'el כִּסָּה = to cover). They are feminine because דֶּרֶךְ and לְבֵנִים are feminine. Without vowels, בעלים here is "with leaves", but the same letters (and even the same vowels, בְּעָלִים) also mean "owners". Only context tells you which.

s.line: and the walking was not at all good.

w: שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ|that has|~lit. that there is in it
s.line: There were few birds in this part of the forest, for birds love the open country where there is plenty of sunshine.
s.note: צִפּוֹר (bird) is feminine, so the verb is אוֹהֲבוֹת. פָּתוּחַ (open) is the pa'ul participle of פָּתַח, "opened", just like סָגוּר (closed) from סָגַר.

s.line: But now and then there came a deep growl from some wild animal hidden among the trees.
s.note: מִדֵּי פַּעַם = from time to time, now and then; very common. נִשְׁמַע (nif'al) = was heard, the passive of שָׁמַע; English "there came a growl" becomes "a growl was heard". You'll also hear מָה נִשְׁמָע? = "what's up?" (lit. what is heard?). In הִסְתַּתֵּר (to hide oneself) the ת of hitpa'el swaps places with the first root letter ס.

s.line: These sounds made the little girl’s heart beat fast, for she did not know what made them;
s.note: גָּרַם לְ־X לְ־ + infinitive = caused X to …: הַגֶּשֶׁם גָּרַם לָנוּ לְאַחֵר (the rain made us late). הִשְׁמִיעַ (hif'il of the same root as שָׁמַע) = to make heard, to produce a sound.

s.line: but Toto knew, and he walked close to Dorothy’s side, and did not even bark in return.
s.note: צָמוּד לְ… = right next to, attached to (a pa'ul participle: "stuck to"). In Israel a רֶכֶב צָמוּד is a company car "attached" to an employee.

w: עַד שֶׁנֵּצֵא|until we get out|pa'al · י־צ־א
s.line: “How long will it be,” the child asked of the Tin Woodman, “before we are out of the forest?”
s.note: כַּמָּה זְמַן זֶה יִקַּח? = how long will it take? (לָקַח = to take, also of time). Note that שָׁאַל takes a direct object: שָׁאֲלָה אֶת אִישׁ הַפַּח = she asked the Tin Woodman, with no word for "of".

s.line: “I cannot tell,” was the answer, “for I have never been to the Emerald City.
But my father went there once, when I was a boy, and he said it was a long journey through a dangerous country,
s.note: מְסֻכָּן (dangerous) is a pu'al participle used as an ordinary adjective, like מְאֻשָּׁר; the noun is סַכָּנָה (danger). In reported speech Hebrew keeps the tense of the original words: אָמַר שֶׁזֶּה מַסָּע "said that it is a journey", where English says "was".

s.line: although nearer to the city where Oz dwells the country is beautiful.
s.note: הָעִיר שֶׁבָּהּ גָּר אוֹז = "the city in which Oz lives". עִיר is feminine, so it is בָּהּ. Everyday speech also says הָעִיר שֶׁאוֹז גָּר בָּהּ, with בָּהּ at the end.

s.line: But I am not afraid so long as I have my oil-can, and nothing can hurt the Scarecrow,
s.note: כָּל עוֹד = as long as: כָּל עוֹד אַתָּה כָּאן (as long as you're here). פָּגַע בְּ־ = to hurt, harm, hit; it takes בְּ: לִפְגֹּעַ בַּדַּחְלִיל. The noun פְּגִיעָה (injury, offense) is common in the news.

s.line: while you bear upon your forehead the mark of the Good Witch’s kiss, and that will protect you from harm.”
s.note: הֵגֵן עַל (hif'il) = to protect; it takes עַל: יָגֵן עָלַיִךְ = will protect you (fem.). The same root gives מָגֵן = shield, as in מָגֵן דָּוִד. סִימָן is masculine, so "it" is הוּא.

s.line: “But Toto!” said the girl anxiously.
s.note: בִּדְאָגָה = "with worry", anxiously. בְּ + a noun is a common way to make an adverb: בְּשִׂמְחָה (gladly), בִּזְהִירוּת (carefully).

s.line: “What will protect him?”
“We must protect him ourselves if he is in danger,” replied the Tin Woodman.
s.note: הִצְטָרֵךְ (hitpa'el of צָרִיךְ) = to need to, have to. When the root starts with צ, the hitpa'el ת swaps places with it and turns into ט: נִצְטָרֵךְ, not ×נִתְצָרֵךְ. After אִם about the future, Hebrew uses the future: אִם הוּא יִהְיֶה, "if he will be".

s.line: Just as he spoke there came from the forest a terrible roar,
and the next moment a great Lion bounded into the road.
s.note: זִנֵּק (pi'el) = to leap, spring. In the news it is used for prices: הַמְּחִירִים זִנְּקוּ = prices soared. Hebrew often puts the verb before the subject when something new appears: זִנֵּק … אַרְיֵה.

s.line: With one blow of his paw he sent the Scarecrow spinning over and over to the edge of the road,
s.note: הֵעִיף is the hif'il of עָף (to fly): "to make fly, send flying". In slang it also means to kick someone out: הֵעִיפוּ אוֹתוֹ מֵהָעֲבוֹדָה (he got fired). הִתְגַּלְגֵּל (to roll) comes from the four-letter root ג־ל־ג־ל, as in גַּלְגַּל (wheel).

s.line: and then he struck at the Tin Woodman with his sharp claws.
But, to the Lion’s surprise, he could make no impression on the tin, although the Woodman fell over in the road and lay still.
s.note: לְהַפְתָּעָתוֹ שֶׁל הָאַרְיֵה = to the Lion's surprise (לְהַפְתָּעָתִי = to my surprise). אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁ = although; in speech it is often shortened to אַף שֶׁ or replaced by לַמְרוֹת שֶׁ. הִצְלִיחַ + infinitive = to manage to, succeed in.

w: הָיָה לוֹ|he had|~lit. there was to him
s.line: Little Toto, now that he had an enemy to face, ran barking toward the Lion,
s.note: הִתְמוֹדֵד עִם = to face, cope with, deal with: one of the most common verbs in modern Hebrew (קָשֶׁה לְהִתְמוֹדֵד עִם זֶה = it's hard to deal with). In elections, מִתְמוֹדֵד = a candidate. לְעֵבֶר = toward.

s.line: and the great beast had opened his mouth to bite the dog,

w: בְּכָל הַכֹּחַ|as hard as she could|~lit. with all the strength
s.line: when Dorothy, fearing Toto would be killed, and heedless of danger, rushed forward and slapped the Lion upon his nose as hard as she could, while she cried out:
s.note: יֵהָרֵג is the nif'al future of הָרַג (to kill): "would be killed", in the future after a verb of fearing. סָטַר לְ־ = to slap someone; it takes לְ, not אֶת: סָטְרָה לָאַרְיֵה. The noun is סְטִירָה (a slap); סְטִירַת לֶחִי = a slap in the face, also figuratively.

s.line: “Don’t you dare to bite Toto!
s.note: אַל תָּעֵז! = don't you dare! From עָז (bold, strong); הֶעָזָה = daring, nerve. אַל + future is the normal negative command.

s.line: You ought to be ashamed of yourself, a big beast like you, to bite a poor little dog!”
s.note: הִתְבַּיֵּשׁ (hitpa'el) = to be ashamed, also to be shy. Parents say תִּתְבַּיֵּשׁ לְךָ! = shame on you! The noun is בּוּשָׁה (shame), which comes up again below.

s.line: “I didn’t bite him,” said the Lion, as he rubbed his nose with his paw where Dorothy had hit it.
s.note: הִכָּה (hif'il, root נ־כ־ה) = to hit, strike; מַכָּה = a blow, from the same root. The נ of the root drops out and leaves a dagesh in כ: הִכְּתָה = she hit.

s.line: “No, but you tried to,” she retorted.
s.note: הֵשִׁיב (hif'il of שָׁב, to return) = to reply, "to give back" an answer. It is a little more literary than עָנָה; it also means to return something: הֵשִׁיב אֶת הַכֶּסֶף.

s.line: “You are nothing but a big coward.”
s.note: סְתָם = just, merely, for no reason; one of the most used words in spoken Hebrew: סְתָם! = just kidding!, סְתָם כָּכָה = for no reason. פַּחְדָּן = coward, from פַּחַד (fear). The ending ־ָן marks a person with a trait: שַׁקְרָן (liar), בַּיְשָׁן (shy person).

s.line: “I know it,” said the Lion, hanging his head in shame.
“I’ve always known it.
But how can I help it?”
s.note: מָה אֲנִי יָכוֹל לַעֲשׂוֹת? ("what can I do?") is the usual way to say "I can't help it". Shorter still: מָה לַעֲשׂוֹת?. Hebrew has no separate perfect tense: "I've always known" is simply תָּמִיד יָדַעְתִּי.

s.line: “I don’t know, I’m sure.
To think of your striking a stuffed man, like the poor Scarecrow!”
s.note: מְמֻלָּא (stuffed) is the pu'al participle of מִלֵּא (pi'el, to fill). It is also the menu word for stuffed food: פִּלְפֵּל מְמֻלָּא (stuffed pepper). לַחְשֹׁב שֶׁ…! at the start of a sentence = "to think that …!", an exclamation of indignation.

s.line: “Is he stuffed?” asked the Lion in surprise,
as he watched her pick up the Scarecrow and set him upon his feet, while she patted him into shape again.
s.note: After הִסְתַּכֵּל אֵיךְ (watched how) Hebrew uses the present, מְרִימָה … מַעֲמִידָה … טוֹפַחַת, for an action seen as it happens. הֶעֱמִיד (hif'il of עָמַד, to stand) = to make stand, set upright; הֵרִים (hif'il of ר־ו־ם) = to lift, pick up.

w: בָּרוּר שֶׁ|of course|~lit. it is clear that
s.line: “Of course he’s stuffed,” replied Dorothy, who was still angry.
s.note: בָּרוּר שֶׁ… = of course, obviously (lit. "it's clear that"). On its own, בָּרוּר! = sure! Hebrew uses a verb for "to be angry": כָּעַס, כָּעֲסָה; it takes עַל: הִיא כָּעֲסָה עָלָיו.

s.line: “That’s why he went over so easily,” remarked the Lion.
“It astonished me to see him whirl around so.
s.note: נִדְהַם (nif'al) = to be astonished; מַדְהִים (hif'il participle, "astonishing") is the everyday word for "amazing": הַסֶּרֶט הָיָה מַדְהִים. מִסְתּוֹבֵב = turning around; colloquially also "hanging around": הוּא מִסְתּוֹבֵב בָּעִיר.

s.line: Is the other one stuffed also?”
“No,” said Dorothy, “he’s made of tin.”
s.note: עָשׂוּי מִ… = made of …, a pa'ul participle of עָשָׂה: הַשֻּׁלְחָן עָשׂוּי מֵעֵץ (the table is made of wood). Before a noun it can also mean "likely to": הוּא עָשׂוּי לְהַגִּיעַ (he may come).

s.line: And she helped the Woodman up again.
“That’s why he nearly blunted my claws,” said the Lion.
s.note: הִקְהָה לִי אֶת הַטְּפָרִים = "blunted my claws", lit. "blunted to me the claws". Hebrew often shows whose body part is affected with לְ + pronoun: שָׁבַר לִי אֶת הַיָּד (he broke my arm). קֵהֶה = blunt.

s.line: “When they scratched against the tin it made a cold shiver run down my back.
s.note: עָבְרָה לִי צְמַרְמֹרֶת = a shiver went through me. You'll hear it of fear or excitement: קִבַּלְתִּי צְמַרְמֹרֶת = I got goosebumps.

s.line: What is that little animal you are so tender of?”
s.note: דָּאַג לְ… = to take care of, look after: הִיא דּוֹאֶגֶת לַיְּלָדִים. With מִ or שֶׁ it means "to worry": אַל תִּדְאַג! = don't worry! חַיָּה is feminine, so זֹאת … הַזֹּאת … לָהּ.

s.line: “He is my dog, Toto,” answered Dorothy.
“Is he made of tin, or stuffed?” asked the Lion.
s.note: אוֹ שֶׁ… ("or that …") is how speakers usually offer the second option in a question: אַתָּה בָּא, אוֹ שֶׁאַתָּה נִשְׁאָר? (are you coming, or are you staying?).

w: לֹא זֶה וְלֹא זֶה|neither|~lit. not this and not this
s.line: “Neither.
s.note: לֹא זֶה וְלֹא זֶה = neither one nor the other. For people: לֹא הוּא וְלֹא הִיא (neither he nor she).

s.line: He’s a—a—a meat dog,” said the girl.
“Oh! He’s a curious animal and seems remarkably small, now that I look at him.
s.note: מְשֻׁנֶּה (strange, odd; fem. מְשֻׁנָּה) has the form of a pu'al participle, from the root of שׁוֹנֶה (different) and שִׁנָּה (changed). בְּמִיּוּחָד = especially, particularly; מְיֻחָד = special.

w: אַף אֶחָד|no one|~with לֹא: no one
s.line: No one would think of biting such a little thing, except a coward like me,” continued the Lion sadly.
s.note: הָיָה חוֹשֵׁב: הָיָה + participle can mean a past habit ("used to"), but here it is the conditional "would think". הִמְשִׁיךְ (hif'il) = to continue; הֶמְשֵׁךְ = continuation, sequel, and בְּהֶמְשֵׁךְ = later on.

s.line: “What makes you a coward?” asked Dorothy,
s.note: מָה הוֹפֵךְ אוֹתְךָ לְ…? = what makes you (into) …? הָפַךְ X לְ־Y = to turn X into Y; הָפַךְ לְ… with no object = to become: הוּא הָפַךְ לְכוֹכָב (he became a star).

s.line: looking at the great beast in wonder, for he was as big as a small horse.
“It’s a mystery,” replied the Lion.
s.note: תַּעֲלוּמָה = a mystery, a riddle; a slightly higher-register word that you'll meet in news and detective stories: הַתַּעֲלוּמָה נִפְתְּרָה (the mystery was solved).

s.line: “I suppose I was born that way.
s.note: נוֹלַד (was born) is the nif'al of יָלַד (to give birth); יוֹם הוּלֶדֶת (birthday) is from the same root. כַּנִּרְאֶה = apparently, probably (lit. "as is seen").

s.line: All the other animals in the forest naturally expect me to be brave, for the Lion is everywhere thought to be the King of Beasts.
s.note: צִפָּה מִ־X לְ… (pi'el) = to expect X to …: מְצַפִּים מִמְּךָ לָבוֹא (you're expected to come). חוֹשְׁבִים with no subject = "people think", Hebrew's way around the English passive "is thought to be". אַמִּיץ (brave) and אֹמֶץ (courage) share a root.

s.line: I learned that if I roared very loudly every living thing was frightened and got out of my way.
s.note: פִּנָּה (pi'el) = to clear, vacate: לְפַנּוֹת אֶת הַדֶּרֶךְ (to make way), לְפַנּוֹת אֶת הַשֻּׁלְחָן (to clear the table). As in reported speech, the "learned that" clause keeps the present tense: שׁוֹאֵג … נִבְהָל … מְפַנֶּה.

s.line: Whenever I’ve met a man I’ve been awfully scared;
s.note: נוֹרָא is "terrible", but in speech it is also an adverb meaning "terribly, really": נוֹרָא יָפֶה (really nice), פָּחַדְתִּי נוֹרָא (I was awfully scared).

s.line: but I just roared at him, and he has always run away as fast as he could go.
s.note: שָׁאַג עַל = to roar at; likewise צָעַק עַל = to yell at someone. הֲכִי מַהֵר שֶׁ… = as fast as …; הֲכִי (most) also makes everyday superlatives: הֲכִי טוֹב (the best).

w: הָיִיתִי בּוֹרֵחַ|I would have run|pa'al ptc · ב־ר־ח
s.line: If the elephants and the tigers and the bears had ever tried to fight me, I should have run myself—I’m such a coward;
s.note: An "if it had happened" sentence: אִם … הָיוּ מְנַסִּים …, הָיִיתִי בּוֹרֵחַ, with הָיָה + participle in both halves. נִלְחַם בְּ־ (nif'al, active meaning) = to fight against; מִלְחָמָה = war, from the same root.

w: בָּרֶגַע שֶׁ|as soon as|~lit. at the moment that
s.line: but just as soon as they hear me roar they all try to get away from me, and of course I let them go.”
s.note: נָתַן לְ־X לְ… = to let X do …: תֵּן לִי לַחְשֹׁב (let me think). בָּרֶגַע שֶׁ… = the moment that, as soon as.

s.line: “But that isn’t right.
The King of Beasts shouldn’t be a coward,” said the Scarecrow.
s.note: אָמוּר לְ… = supposed to, a pa'ul participle of אָמַר ("said"): הָאוֹטוֹבּוּס אָמוּר לְהַגִּיעַ (the bus is supposed to come). בְּסֵדֶר = OK, all right; זֶה לֹא בְּסֵדֶר = that's not right, that's not fair.

s.line: “I know it,” returned the Lion, wiping a tear from his eye with the tip of his tail.
s.note: נִגֵּב (pi'el) = to wipe dry: לְנַגֵּב אֶת הַיָּדַיִם (to dry your hands); מַגֶּבֶת = towel. בִּקְצֵה is the construct of קָצֶה (tip, end) with בְּ.

w: מְמָרֵר לִי אֶת הַחַיִּים|makes my life miserable|~idiom: lit. embitters my life
s.line: “It is my great sorrow, and makes my life very unhappy.
s.note: מְמָרֵר לִי אֶת הַחַיִּים = "makes my life bitter", a living idiom for making someone miserable: הַשָּׁכֵן מְמָרֵר לָנוּ אֶת הַחַיִּים (the neighbor makes our lives miserable). The root is מ־ר־ר, as in מַר (bitter).

s.line: But whenever there is danger, my heart begins to beat fast.”
“Perhaps you have heart disease,” said the Tin Woodman.
s.note: מַחֲלַת לֵב = heart disease, the construct of מַחֲלָה (disease), with ה becoming ת. חוֹלֶה = sick, from the same root.

w: יָכוֹל לִהְיוֹת|it may be|~fixed phrase: maybe
s.line: “It may be,” said the Lion.
s.note: יָכוֹל לִהְיוֹת = could be, maybe; always in this masculine form, whatever it refers to. יָכוֹל לִהְיוֹת שֶׁהוּא צוֹדֵק = he may be right.

s.line: “If you have,” continued the Tin Woodman, “you ought to be glad, for it proves you have a heart.
s.note: הוֹכִיחַ (hif'il) = to prove; הוֹכָחָה = proof. In older Hebrew it also meant "to rebuke". Hebrew uses a verb for "to be glad": שָׂמַח, לִשְׂמֹחַ.

w: לִהְיוֹת לִי|I have|~lit. be to me
s.line: For my part, I have no heart; so I cannot have heart disease.”
s.note: לְגַבַּי = as for me, regarding me; לְגַבֵּי + noun = about, regarding: מָה לְגַבֵּי מָחָר? (what about tomorrow?). In לֹא יְכוֹלָה לִהְיוֹת לִי מַחֲלָה the verb is feminine to agree with מַחֲלָה, the thing "had".

w: הָיָה לִי|I had|~lit. there was to me
s.line: “Perhaps,” said the Lion thoughtfully, “if I had no heart I should not be a coward.”
s.note: מְהֻרְהָר = pensive, deep in thought, a pu'al participle from הִרְהֵר (to ponder, muse). הִרְהוּרִים = musings, second thoughts.

s.line: “Have you brains?” asked the Scarecrow.
s.note: A yes/no question in Hebrew is just a statement with a rising voice: <t>יֵשׁ לְךָ מֹחַ?</t> = do you have a brain? Hebrew uses the singular <t>מֹחַ</t> where Baum writes "brains".

s.line: “I suppose so.
s.note: הֵנִיחַ (hif'il) = to put down, and also to assume: אֲנִי מְנִיחַ שֶׁכֵּן = I suppose so; הַנָּחָה = an assumption. שֶׁכֵּן / שֶׁלֹּא = that yes / that not: אֲנִי חוֹשֵׁב שֶׁלֹּא (I don't think so).

s.line: I’ve never looked to see,” replied the Lion.
“I am going to the Great Oz to ask him to give me some,” remarked the Scarecrow, “for my head is stuffed with straw.”
s.note: בִּקֵּשׁ מִ־X שֶׁ… = to ask X to …: "ask" takes מִ ("request from"), and the request goes in a שֶׁ clause with the future: בִּקַּשְׁתִּי מִמֶּנּוּ שֶׁיָּבוֹא (I asked him to come). To ask a question is a different verb: שָׁאַל.

s.line: “And I am going to ask him to give me a heart,” said the Woodman.
“And I am going to ask him to send Toto and me back to Kansas,” added Dorothy.
s.note: הֶחֱזִיר (hif'il of חָזַר, to return) = to bring or send back: תַּחֲזִיר לִי אֶת הַסֵּפֶר (give me back the book). הוֹסִיף (hif'il) = to add; תּוֹסֶפֶת = an addition, an extra. Here הוֹלֵךְ / הוֹלֶכֶת is literal: they really are walking to Oz.

s.line: “Do you think Oz could give me courage?” asked the Cowardly Lion.
s.note: יוּכַל is the future of יָכוֹל (can): אוּכַל, תּוּכַל, יוּכַל. תּוּכַל לַעֲזֹר לִי? = could you help me? The Lion asks all of them, so "you" is plural: אַתֶּם חוֹשְׁבִים.

s.line: “Just as easily as he could give me brains,” said the Scarecrow.
s.note: בְּאוֹתָהּ קַלּוּת = with the same ease; אוֹתָהּ before a noun means "the same". קַלּוּת (ease) comes from קַל (easy, light); בְּקַלּוּת = easily.

s.line: “Or give me a heart,” said the Tin Woodman.
“Or send me back to Kansas,” said Dorothy.

w: אִם לֹא אִכְפַּת לָכֶם|if you don't mind|~idiom
s.line: “Then, if you don’t mind, I’ll go with you,” said the Lion, “for my life is simply unbearable without a bit of courage.”
s.note: אִכְפַּת לְ… = to care, mind: לֹא אִכְפַּת לִי (I don't care), אִכְפַּת לְךָ? (do you mind?). בִּלְתִּי נִסְבָּל = unbearable: נִסְבָּל (nif'al participle) = "bearable", from סָבַל (to suffer, bear), and בִּלְתִּי = un-. חַיִּים is plural, so the adjective is too.

s.line: “You will be very welcome,” answered Dorothy, “for you will help to keep away the other wild beasts.
s.note: נִשְׂמַח שֶׁתָּבוֹא = "we'll be glad if you come", a warm way to say "you're welcome to come". הִרְחִיק (hif'il of רָחוֹק, far) = to keep away, distance: הַרְחֵק מִשָּׁם! (stay well away from there).

s.line: It seems to me they must be more cowardly than you are if they allow you to scare them so easily.”
s.note: נִרְאֶה לִי = it seems to me, I think; very common in speech. בֶּטַח = surely, probably; בֶּטַח! alone = sure! חַיּוֹת is feminine plural, so: הֵן … פַּחְדָּנִיּוֹת … נוֹתְנוֹת … אוֹתָן. הִפְחִיד (hif'il) = to frighten, the causative of פָּחַד.

s.line: “They really are,” said the Lion, “but that doesn’t make me any braver,
and as long as I know myself to be a coward I shall be unhappy.”
s.note: אֻמְלָל = miserable, wretched; stronger than עָצוּב (sad).

s.line: So once more the little company set off upon the journey,
s.note: יָצָא לַדֶּרֶךְ = to set out, "go out to the road". The phrase is also used for projects: הַפְּרוֹיֶקְט יָצָא לַדֶּרֶךְ (the project got under way). חֲבוּרָה = a group of companions, from the root of חָבֵר (friend).

s.line: the Lion walking with stately strides at Dorothy’s side.
s.note: לְצִדָּהּ שֶׁל דּוֹרוֹתִי = at Dorothy's side: the suffix points ahead to the owner named after שֶׁל, as in אִשְׁתּוֹ שֶׁל הַחַקְלַאי. מַלְכוּתִי = royal, regal, from מֶלֶךְ.

s.line: Toto did not approve of this new comrade at first, for he could not forget how nearly he had been crushed between the Lion’s great jaws.
s.note: מְרֻצֶּה מִ… = pleased with, satisfied with, a pu'al participle from the root of רָצָה (to want): אֲנִי מְרֻצֶּה מֵהַתּוֹצָאוֹת (I'm pleased with the results). לְהִמָּחֵץ = to be crushed, the nif'al infinitive of מָחַץ. In nif'al infinitives and futures the נ disappears and leaves a dagesh in the first root letter.

s.line: But after a time he became more at ease, and presently Toto and the Cowardly Lion had grown to be good friends.
s.note: נִרְגַּע (nif'al, active meaning) = to calm down; תֵּרָגַע! = calm down! הִרְגִּיעַ (hif'il) = to calm someone. זְמַן מָה = some time, a while: מָה after a noun means "some".

s.line: During the rest of that day there was no other adventure to mar the peace of their journey.
s.note: הִפְרִיעַ לְ… (hif'il) = to disturb, bother; it takes לְ: אֲנִי לֹא רוֹצֶה לְהַפְרִיעַ לְךָ (I don't want to disturb you). הַרְפַּתְקָה is feminine, so הָיְתָה and אַחֶרֶת.

s.line: Once, indeed, the Tin Woodman stepped upon a beetle that was crawling along the road, and killed the poor little thing.
s.note: דָּרַךְ עַל = to step on, and דֶּרֶךְ = road: the same three letters, דרך, in one sentence. Without vowels you tell them apart by their place in the sentence. אָמְנָם = it's true, admittedly; usually followed by אֲבָל.

s.line: This made the Tin Woodman very unhappy, for he was always careful not to hurt any living creature;
s.note: הֶעֱצִיב (hif'il) = to make sad, the causative of עָצוּב (sad). נִזְהַר (nif'al, active meaning) = to be careful; תִּזָּהֵר! = be careful!, and זָהִיר = careful.

s.line: and as he walked along he wept several tears of sorrow and regret.
s.note: תּוֹךְ כְּדֵי + noun = while (doing): תּוֹךְ כְּדֵי נְסִיעָה (while driving). הִזִּיל דְּמָעוֹת = to shed tears; נוֹזֵל (liquid) is from the same root. חֲרָטָה = regret, remorse; הִתְחָרֵט = to regret.

s.line: These tears ran slowly down his face and over the hinges of his jaw, and there they rusted.
s.note: זָלַג = to trickle, run down (of tears); in the news, הַמֵּידָע זָלַג = the information leaked. הֶחֱלִיד (hif'il) = to rust, from חֲלוּדָה (rust). צִיר = hinge; it also means "axis".

s.line: When Dorothy presently asked him a question the Tin Woodman could not open his mouth, for his jaws were tightly rusted together.
s.note: תָּקוּעַ = stuck, a pa'ul participle of תָּקַע (to stick in, jam). Everyday use: הַמַּחְשֵׁב תָּקוּעַ (the computer is frozen), אֲנִי תָּקוּעַ בַּפְּקָקִים (I'm stuck in traffic). מֵרֹב + noun = from so much …: מֵרֹב צְחוֹק (from laughing so hard).

s.line: He became greatly frightened at this and made many motions to Dorothy to relieve him, but she could not understand.
s.note: סִימֵן (pi'el) = to signal, gesture, also to mark: it comes from סִימָן (sign, mark). סִימֵן לָהּ שֶׁ… + future = signaled to her to …. הֵבִין (hif'il) = to understand; בִּינָה = intelligence, as in בִּינָה מְלָאכוּתִית (artificial intelligence).

w: לֹא בְּסֵדֶר|was wrong|~lit. not in order
s.line: The Lion was also puzzled to know what was wrong.
s.note: מְבֻלְבָּל = confused, mixed up, a pu'al participle of בִּלְבֵּל (to confuse, mix up). בִּלְבּוּל = confusion.

s.line: But the Scarecrow seized the oil-can from Dorothy’s basket and oiled the Woodman’s jaws, so that after a few moments he could talk as well as before.
s.note: חָטַף = to snatch, grab; in the news it means "to kidnap" (חֲטִיפָה = kidnapping), and חָטִיף is a snack. שִׁמֵּן (pi'el) = to oil, grease, a verb made from שֶׁמֶן (oil).

w: יְלַמֵּד אוֹתִי לֶקַח|will teach me a lesson|~idiom
s.line: “This will serve me a lesson,” said he, “to look where I step.
s.note: לִמֵּד לֶקַח = to teach a lesson (often a hard one), and לָמַד לֶקַח = to learn one's lesson. The pi'el לִמֵּד (teach) is the causative partner of pa'al לָמַד (learn).

s.line: For if I should kill another bug or beetle I should surely cry again, and crying rusts my jaws so that I cannot speak.”
s.note: After אִם about a possible future event Hebrew uses the future: אִם אֶהֱרֹג … אֶבְכֶּה (if I kill … I will cry). חֶרֶק = insect, the general word; a חִפּוּשִׁית is a beetle. בְּכִי = crying, from בָּכָה (to cry).

s.line: Thereafter he walked very carefully, with his eyes on the road,
s.note: בִּזְהִירוּת = carefully, "with care" (זְהִירוּת = caution, from the root of נִזְהַר). The road sign זְהִירוּת! = caution! מֵאָז = since then, from then on.

s.line: and when he saw a tiny ant toiling by he would step over it, so as not to harm it.
s.note: הָיָה פּוֹסֵעַ = "he would step", a repeated habit in the past (הָיָה + participle). עָמַל = to toil, labor; עָמָל = hard work. זָעִיר = tiny, a slightly literary word for קְטַנְטַן. נְמָלָה is feminine, so מֵעָלֶיהָ and בָּהּ.

s.line: The Tin Woodman knew very well he had no heart, and therefore he took great care never to be cruel or unkind to anything.
s.note: הִקְפִּיד (hif'il) = to be careful to, insist on: הוּא מַקְפִּיד לְהַגִּיעַ בַּזְּמַן (he makes a point of arriving on time); הִקְפִּיד עַל = to be strict about. לְעוֹלָם לֹא = never, mostly with the future or an infinitive; אַף פַּעַם לֹא is the everyday equivalent.

s.line: “You people with hearts,” he said, “have something to guide you, and need never do wrong;
s.note: הִדְרִיךְ (hif'il) = to guide, show the way, from the root of דֶּרֶךְ (way). מַדְרִיךְ = a guide, instructor, youth-group counselor; הַדְרָכָה = guidance, training.

s.line: but I have no heart, and so I must be very careful.
s.note: חַיָּב = must, have to; stronger than צָרִיךְ. It also means "owing": אַתָּה חַיָּב לִי כֶּסֶף (you owe me money).

s.line: When Oz gives me a heart of course I needn’t mind so much.”
s.note: כְּשֶׁאוֹז יִתֵּן: after כְּשֶׁ about the future Hebrew uses the future ("when Oz will give"), where English uses the present "gives": כְּשֶׁאַגִּיעַ, אֶתְקַשֵּׁר (when I arrive, I'll call).
